stories.headline: Seahawks take Week 1 win over Patriots, lose QB Darnold early
stories.summary: In a Super Bowl LX rematch, the Seahawks kicked off the NFL season with a win but lost QB Sam Darnold to a hip injury.
stories.body:
SEATTLE -- The Seattle Seahawks beat the New England Patriots 13-10 on Wednesday night in a Super Bowl LX rematch.

As the Seahawks prepared for their quest to become only the third team this century to repeat as Super Bowl champions, they didn't talk about "defending" their title or trying to "run it back." They wanted to remain forward-looking, knowing it's a new season and a new team that will face new challenges.

No one could have predicted the timing and potential magnitude of the challenge that hit them in their opener. On the first series, quarterback Sam Darnold went down for the remainder of the game -- and potentially beyond -- with an injury to his right hip. Backup quarterback Drew Lock stepped up and the defense took over the second half, forcing Patriots QB Drake Maye to turn the ball over three times in the fourth quarter.

Sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter that Darnold was at Harborview Medical Center in Seattle, undergoing a CT scan on his hip. The initial test was encouraging but inconclusive, and Darnold now is scheduled to undergo an MRI on Thursday. Coach Mike Macdonald said postgame that initial tests seem to show the QB avoided a fracture.

Here are the most important things to know for both teams:

Seattle Seahawks (1-0)

What to make of Drew Lock's performance: Lock went 16-of-22 for 187 passing yards and one TD. He played as well as the Seahawks could have expected -- maybe better -- considering he was pressed into action early in the game. He kept the ball out of harm's way and made big-time throws, including a 21-yard strike to Jaxon Smith-Njigba that nearly converted a third-and-22. New coordinator Brian Fleury showed faith in his backup quarterback by opting against a tush push with tight end AJ Barner on the fourth-and-1 play that resulted in Lock's touchdown pass to Smith-Njigba. The Seahawks did not help Lock out with three false start penalties.

Trend to watch: As expected, the Seahawks went with a committee approach in their backfield. Rookie first-round Jadarian Price led the way, and he flashed explosiveness while gaining 52 yards on 10 carries. He might have gotten more work if not for the offensive penalties that forced Seattle into passing situations. George Holani gained 29 yards on eight carries, while Emanuel Wilson added 3 yards on two attempts. This is how the work figures to be split for at least the first four games while Zach Charbonnet begins the season on the physically unable to perform list.

Most surprising performance: Cornerback Nehemiah Pritchett's fourth-quarter interception on a tipped pass got the Seahawks the ball for what would be their tying touchdown drive. He had an earlier pass breakup as well. The third-year pro is serving as the Seahawks' No. 3 corner, which has looked like the biggest question mark on a defense that allowed the fewest points in the NFL last season. He'll face competition for that job from Trevon Diggs and potentially Terrion Arnold (who's on the commissioner's exempt list) as well. But plays like that one will keep him in the starting lineup.

Next game: at Arizona Cardinals (Sunday, Sept. 20, at 4:25 p.m. ET)

New England Patriots (0-1)
Wide receiver A.J. Brown was knocked out of the game in the third quarter with a right ankle injury, taking away quarterback Drake Maye's No. 1 option and creating uncertainty about how long the team might be without him.

Maye missed him greatly, with the Patriots losing a 10-0 lead as the Seahawks fed off two Maye interceptions and then sealed the game with a third. The first pick came when Maye threw downfield to Romeo Doubs while giving the receiver a chance to climb the ladder, something he had shown a knack for in training camp. Doubs later had a costly drop on a play that would have gone for a first down but instead was followed by Maye's second interception when he was looking for receiver Pop Douglas over the middle on third-and-14.

The Seahawks scored on the ensuing drive both times -- with a touchdown and a field goal. Then they closed out the game with the final pick.

What to make of Drake Maye's performance: Maye threw multiple interceptions, which is rare. He had only one game last season (including playoffs) in which he threw two interceptions -- the Super Bowl vs. the Seahawks. The Patriots played it conservatively early, as he had just one pass traveling more than 10 air yards in the first half, according to ESPN Analytics tracking. Maye's other 11 throws traveled a combined 15 air yards. That might have been designed, in part, to protect the offensive line. Two of Maye's interceptions in the second half were on downfield throws.

Most surprising performance: Doubs. The Patriots signed the former Packers receiver to a four-year, $68 million contract as a free agent in the offseason, and he was involved in two critical plays that hurt the team -- Maye's first interception and a dropped pass when he was open to convert a first down that preceded the second pick. The Patriots needed Doubs to deliver after Brown left the game with a right ankle injury early in the third quarter.

Stat to know: Rookie tight end Eli Raridon, who scored the opening touchdown of the NFL season on a 2-yard pass from Maye, did not score a TD in 12 games with Notre Dame last season.

Next game: vs. Pittsburgh Steelers (Sunday, Sept. 20, at 1 p.m. ET)

stories.headline: Valdez homers and the Pirates use 8 pitchers in a 4-2 win over the White Sox
stories.summary: — Rookie Esmerlyn Valdez hit a solo shot, rookie Konnor Griffin singled in two runs in Pittsburgh’s three-run seventh inning and the Pirates held on to beat the Chicago White Sox 4-2 on Wednesday night for their third straight victory.
stories.body:
CHICAGO -- — Rookie Esmerlyn Valdez hit a solo shot, rookie Konnor Griffin singled in two runs in Pittsburgh’s three-run seventh inning and the Pirates held on to beat the Chicago White Sox 4-2 on Wednesday night for their third straight victory.


Rafael Flores Jr. added an RBI single to help the Pirates win for the eighth time in 10 games to climb back to .500.


Pittsburgh used eight pitchers to hand the White Sox a second straight loss and their seventh in their last 10. AL Central-leading Chicago (75-70) maintained a two-game lead over Cleveland, which lost at Baltimore.


The benches and bullpens emptied in the seventh, but order was quickly restored.


Yohan Ramirez, Pittsburgh's sixth pitcher, entered and got Miguel Vargas to ground into an inning-ending double play with the bases loaded and the Pirates head 4-1. Sam Antonacci elbowed Brandon Lowe at second as he came up from his slide to set off the fracas.


Antonacci’s RBI infield single had driven in Chicago's first run.


White Sox slugger Munetaka Murakami hit his 31st homer in the eighth to cut it to 4-2, but struck out in his first two times at the plate, running his streak of strikeouts to eight straight plate appearances. Murakami was hit by a pitch from Gregory Soto in his third time up.


The White Sox loaded the bases off Luke Weaver with one out in the eighth, but Chase Meidroth lined to third for an inning-ending double-play.


Pirates opener Lake Bachar got the first five outs. Brandon Eisert (3-2) followed with 2 1/3 innings of hitless ball, striking out five, for the win. Carmen Mlodzinski, Soto, Camilo Doval, Ramirez and Weaver followed before Mason Montgomery pitched a 1-2-3 ninth for his 11th save


White Sox starter Davis Martin (9-7) allowed one run, on Valdez’s 17th homer in the fifth, and four hits in five innings in his second start since coming off the injured list from a tight middle finger blister.


Up next
Pirates RHP Jared Jones (3-6, 4.46 ERA) was set to start against White Sox LHP Hagen Smith (3-1, 0.56) on Thursday in the series finale.

stories.headline: Barry Melrose, former player, coach and ESPN analyst, dies
stories.summary: Barry Melrose, the former NHL player and coach who was a beloved, longtime hockey analyst for ESPN, died Wednesday, his wife, Cindy, told ESPN's Steve Levy.
stories.body:
Barry Melrose, a former NHL player and coach who was a beloved hockey analyst for ESPN for over 25 years, died Wednesday, his wife, Cindy, told ESPN's Steve Levy.

He was 70.

Melrose was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in 2023, leading to his retirement from ESPN. He joined the network in 1996.

"For decades, Barry Melrose was one of the most distinctive and trusted voices in hockey," ESPN said in a statement. "His knowledge of the game was deep, his candor was refreshing, and his passion was unmistakable. He was a foundational part of ESPN's hockey coverage, and fans and teammates truly appreciated his entertaining delivery and charismatic personality.

"We send our deepest condolences to his loved ones. He always kept it interesting and he will be missed."

Melrose served as coach of the Wayne Gretzky-led Los Angeles Kings, taking them to the Stanley Cup Final in the first of his three seasons (1992 to 1995). He stepped away briefly from ESPN in 2008 to return to the bench, this time as coach of the Tampa Bay Lightning for 16 games.

Overall, he had an 84-108-29 record as a head coach.

At ESPN, millions watched him as a studio analyst, and within the company's walls, he was lauded as the consummate teammate.

He was known for his witty personality, flashy suits and recognizable goatee, slicked-back hair and mullet, which endeared him to hockey fans worldwide. He regularly worked alongside Levy and John Buccigross on ESPN's hockey coverage, including All-Star Games, Stanley Cup playoffs and the Cup Final.

"Barry was my best friend at ESPN," Buccigross wrote on social media Wednesday night. "A big brother figure of rock solid values. I am shook to my core. Barry gave his life to hockey and some of his ESPN family, like me, learned of his shocking death today while at a hockey rink in Las Vegas preparing for the upcoming season. Chilling and fitting -- the rink was Barry's home. A more beloved ESPN institution there has not been. We love you, Barry. Forever."

At the time of Melrose's retirement, Gretzky, The Great One, paid tribute to him with the greatest of compliments: "Hockey is more than a game, it's a community -- a finely tuned orchestra -- and Barry was our conductor."

The Kings hired Melrose in 1992, and with Gretzky leading the way, they made a memorable playoff run, reaching the Cup Final before losing to the Montreal Canadiens in five games.

Rob Blake, a Hockey Hall of Fame defenseman, played for Melrose during that time, and after learning of his death Wednesday, he recalled their days together.

"He was just a terrific person to be in charge of our team," Blake told ESPN. "A real big personality and he was a pleasure. He loved the game of hockey -- the bright lights in L.A. were nothing for him when he got there."

Blake said he wasn't surprised when Melrose made a successful pivot to television.

"What he was teaching us about the game of hockey, he was teaching on TV," Blake said. "He got to promote the game for a number of years at a very high level. It was great."

Tony Granato, another former King, added: "He could light up a room. He could make people hear his voice and then you turn around and wonder what else he was going to say? There was no phoniness to him. He just was himself."

Melrose, who was from rural Kelvington, Saskatchewan, began his coaching career in 1987, when he led the Medicine Hat Tigers to the WHL's Memorial Cup title. He also coached the Seattle Thunderbirds for the 1988-89 season and the Adirondack Red Wings of the American Hockey League for three seasons (1989 to 1992), winning the Calder Cup championship in 1991.

During his 11 years as a player, Melrose appeared in 335 career games as a defenseman in the NHL with the Winnipeg Jets, Toronto Maple Leafs and Detroit Red Wings (1979 to 1986). He also played three seasons with Cincinnati in the WHA (1976 to 1979) -- the last teaming with a young Mark Messier.

He finished with 10 goals, 33 points and 728 penalty minutes in 300 NHL career games. His WHA totals were five goals, 32 points and 343 penalty minutes in 178 games.

"From the flowing locks of his distinctive mullet to the flared lapels of his trademark long suit coats, Barry Melrose cut an unmistakable figure whenever you were fortunate enough to run into him at a rink or catch him on your television screen," NHL commissioner Gary Bettman said. "You were even more fortunate if you engaged him in conversation or listened to his analysis because he never failed to boost your love of the game of hockey."

Melrose is survived by his wife, Cindy, and two sons, Tyrell and Adrien.

ESPN's Greg Wyshynski contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Star veteran joins Bailey in re-signing with Lions
stories.summary: Dual Brisbane premiership hero Dayne Zorko has signed a deal to play on in 2027, putting him in reach of the Lions' all-time games record.
stories.body:
Two days after Zac Bailey confirmed his bumper eight-year deal to stay in Brisbane, veteran premiership teammate Dayne Zorko has inked a new contract to play on in 2027.

Turning 38 before next season starts, Zorko is forging on for a 16th campaign in the AFL.

Not debuting until he was 23 after being overlooked in four-straight drafts, the former Lions captain has the opportunity to break the club's all-time games record.

Saturday's semi-final clash with Adelaide will be Zorko's 319th AFL game.

Barring any major injuries, Zorko will break Lions legend Simon Black's record of 322 games early next year.

If the Lions reach a fourth-straight grand final, the decider will be Zorko's 321st AFL appearance.

After playing all 54 games during the 2024 and 2025 premiership campaigns, Zorko has been restricted to 14 games so far this year due to several soft-tissue injuries.

"The way he continues to perform at 37 years of age is a real credit to his professionalism, preparation and hunger to keep improving," Brisbane football boss Danny Daly said.

"Zorks has been an outstanding player and leader for the Brisbane Lions over a long period of time, and his experience, competitiveness, energy, and leadership remain incredibly important to our group."

AFL/VFL games record holder Scott Pendlebury - who is moving to play with Gold Coast - and Zorko will be the only players left in the AFL born in the 1980s.

stories.headline: UCL talking points: Mourinho's blueprint to win the Champions League
stories.summary: Kylian Mbappé up front and Thibaut Courtois in goal; does Jose Mourinho really need any more than that? ESPN's Mark Ogden, Gab Marcotti, Rob Dawson and Sam Tighe weigh in on all the moments that mattered from Matchday 1 so far.
stories.body:
The 2026-27 UEFA Champions League is officially in full swing with 36 teams across this still-kinda-new league phase playing their opening games across three days. And already, with some Matchday 1 games on Thursday still to come, we have plenty to talk about.

On Tuesday, Manchester City and Real Madrid picked up wins that showed flashes of their respective best, though with questions marks around both teams given unconvincing performances. Then, on Wednesday, Barcelona smashed Feyenoord 5-1, Paris Saint-Germain put six past Slovan Bratislava, Liverpool dug deep to beat Atlético Madrid at Anfield, and Arsenal left it late to finally break down Napoli 1-0 with a Martin Ødegaard goal 10 minutes from the end.

So, what to make of it all? ESPN FC writers Gab Marcotti, Mark Ogden, Rob Dawson and Sam Tighe are here to break down the action as it happened and look ahead to the second legs.

(Editor's Note: We will update this file after Thursday's matches with some fresh talking points to fully take in the whole Matchday.)

- UCL Power Rankings, MD1: Which club is No. 1?

- Haaland can keep Man City on top -- as long as he stays fit

- UCL as it happened: Liverpool hang on to beat Atleti

Q1. REAL MADRID 2-1 INTERNAZIONALE: Once again, Thibaut Courtois saved the day after Los Blancos raced out to a 2-0 lead, with Trent Alexander-Arnold not really working in midfield. Meet the new Real Madrid ... is the same as the old Madrid? Are they really a front-runner at this point, or has Jose Mourinho got a more difficult job on his hands than we first thought?
Marcotti: They won, didn't they? The worst-case scenario is they play like this and with Courtois between the sticks, and ridiculously fast forwards like Kylian Mbappé and Vinícius Júnior up front, they'll always have a chance of winning. That's the bottom line, and I base it more on performance than the game itself.

Yes, Inter Milan outshot them and had 64% possession at the Bernabeu, crucially self-destructing with two craven mistakes that led to Real Madrid's goals. But the basic formula -- Courtois performs magic at one end, one or more stars score at the other -- worked. (And even without Inter's defensive errors, on a normal day, it took some big Josep Martínez saves to keep Madrid out.)

That's the worst-case scenario. The best-case scenario is Mourinho gets this team ticking as it should, finds the right balance up front and at the back, and his big guns deliver. So more than one thing can be true: Mourinho has a difficult job and a long road ahead -- lest we forget, the man just got there and most of his team returned late from the World Cup -- but at the same time, even amid these conditions, they can beat anybody on their day.

Dawson: Real Madrid are always a front-runner. Just look at their team. The expanded league phase is forgiving for the big teams, and they should reach the knockout rounds regardless of their form.

Beyond that, they've got big players who can win games by themselves. No one ever wants to face Real Madrid in the Champions League and that tells its own story.

One of the biggest questions around this version of Real Madrid is Mourinho. He has history in this competition that shouldn't be overlooked, but it's been a while since he was in charge of a truly top team at this level.

Ogden: I don't see a problem here. As Gab says, Real won, and they won against a decent Inter team too. Mourinho won't care about those possession stats, either: I think we've all now accepted that they are a pretty pointless metric because winning teams are happy to let their opponents have the ball so they can sit back and hit them on the counter-attack.

Ultimately, Real are stacked with attacking talent and have a coach who knows how to organise a defence, so they have the ingredients to go all the way. Personally, I would back PSG to beat Real, but they are the only side out there who I would confidently expect to win in any circumstances. On their day, Mourinho's Real could beat Arsenal, Barcelona, Manchester City and Bayern Munich, so yes, they are definitely a front-runner.

Tighe: Surely the worst case scenario is that they lose, Gab? (Ha ha!)

I jest, of course, and without wishing to start the Champions League season off on the wrong foot, Gab has had Madrid nailed for years: Courtois + Mbappé is a formula that can win any game of football, which means it's also a potential recipe for broader success.

However, I also think it's fair to suggest they will come unstuck at some point this season if they are consistently that easy to play against and break down. It's only Matchday 1, so nobody should be sounding the alarm just yet, but if I don't see steady improvement between now and Christmas, I'm not going to have much faith in them when we sit here and make our knockout stage predictions in January.

FC PORTO 0-2 MAN CITY: Erling Haaland was the man yet again for City, scoring twice and leading the early goals race (along with Borussia Dortmund's Serhou Guirassy). That's 59 goals in 59 career Champions League games now, after being the quickest-ever player to reach 50 goals in Europe's top competition. But he needs help, and although Ayyoub Bouaddi was good in midfield, Gianluigi Donnarumma doesn't look like the keeper they need him to be, and the fullbacks were again not good enough. If Haaland stops scoring, how can this team keep going?
Dawson: Haaland is a big question mark for City this season. They've invested around £450 million in the squad this summer, but since Omar Marmoush joined Tottenham Hotspur in the final days of the transfer window, there's no natural replacement if Haaland gets injured.

New City manager Enzo Maresca will have to be clever. He needs Haaland fit and in rhythm as much as possible, but his minutes will have to be carefully managed and Haaland has already hinted that a summer spent at the World Cup is taking its toll.

City have started the season with four straight wins in all competitions, but they are a completely different team without Haaland up front. He's the one player they cannot do without.

Ogden: I was in Porto for the game on Tuesday and one thing that stood out inside Estadio do Dragao was the anticipation among the home supporters whenever the ball was played back to Donnarumma in the City goal. They sensed he was edgy and nervous, and it was only through bad luck on the home side's part that they didn't score from one of the Italy No. 1's errors of judgement.

Maresca said after the game that his players were at fault, not Donnarumma, because they were passing back to him too often. That's an incredible claim, and one that'll play into the hands of opponents who will now target Donnarumma even more.

So what does this all mean? It means that even though Haaland is the deadliest forward in the world, the issue in goal could cost City dearly against a top team, which bears out the old maxim that you are only as strong as your weakest link -- and City's weakness is Donnarumma.

With or without Haaland's goals, City have a problem with their goalkeeper.

Tighe: Donnarumma is a fascinating talking point, because he is both a greatness and a weakness.

We have hard evidence that his miraculous shot-stopping ability can play a pivotal role in winning a Champions League. PSG would not have got past Arsenal in 2024-25 -- heck, they may not have even got past Aston Villa in the round before -- without his heroics. That team found a way to play the best possession football on the planet with him in goal.

It is often said that a goalkeeper just like him can be the match-winning difference on the biggest stage. It's not far off from the Courtois discussion we had with Madrid, is it?

Perhaps the difference here is that as a coach, Maresca is so incredibly dogmatic in his approach and principles that he will end up selling Donnarumma down the river tactically. Meanwhile, Luis Enrique was always willing to make adjustments for the good of the team.

Marcotti: Really? Manchester City win and keep a clean sheet away from home against a team that had lost once at home in the Champions League in the previous four years, and we're talking about how Donnarumma could be a problem? And the reason he's (supposedly) a problem is that he's not as comfortable on the ball as other keepers?

His job is to keep balls out. Francesco Farioli's Porto presses very aggressively and when teams do that, they leave space behind. A big boot up the pitch for Haaland and Antoine Semenyo to chase, and it's Porto -- or anybody else who presses like that -- who'll pay the price. If Donnarumma is City's biggest problem, then they're in a pretty good position.

Maresca isn't stupid; he knows he can't ask or expect Donnarumma to do with the ball at his feet what some other keepers are capable of. He'll adjust.

As for Haaland, that's a more interesting subject. Marmoush isn't really a Haaland substitute, so I don't think it's a big deal that he left. He did his best work in a front two or on the wing rather than as a lone striker anyway.

I am a little surprised they didn't look at replacements, but of course, it's not easy to find a an off-brand Haaland; you're more likely to end up with a different sort of player. I'd imagine when Haaland needs a breather, they can shift Semenyo or Iliman Ndiaye up front. Even Phil Foden could do it. At that point, you're not going to play with a center-forward anyway -- just a guy who can make the right runs at the right time.

Q3. LIVERPOOL 2-1 ATLETICO MADRID: For a while, it followed a familiar script for their meetings: LFC dominate early but fall behind, play catch up the entire time, level the game ... and then when it felt like it would again drift into Diego Simeone's favor, the Reds reversed course and deservedly took all three points. Is this starting to look like the Liverpool side Andoni Iraola is trying to shape? Or were they just lucky for a change?
Dawson: There was a lot to like for Liverpool. Florian Wirtz looked sharp and Bradley Barcola was quick and dangerous. He should have scored at least once, but it was a promising first start.

This is a work in progress for Iraola and it's going to take time. There are signs, though, that at least the attacking phases of play are starting to click.

Liverpool have had a bit of stick for their defensive frailties, but it's now eight goals scored in four games. That's a healthy return for any team, nevermind one still getting to grips with the methods of a new manager.

Ogden: I'm not convinced by the positive tone here. Let's not forget how open and naive Liverpool were in the first half. Overturning a 1-0 deficit to beat Atlético Madrid is a good result on any Champions League night, but I still think Iraola has some big problems to address.

The biggest issue is how to accommodate Dominik Szoboszlai and Wirtz in the same team. Ultimately, I don't think you can. Szoboszlai looks like a player who wants the freedom to roam around the opposition half, but with Wirtz in the side, he can't do that. So, Iraola has to take one of them out. Alexis Mac Allister wants a new contract, but his form last season didn't merit a new deal this summer and his performance against Atlético -- where he was chasing shadows for much of the game and on a disciplinary tightrope after a first-half booking -- highlighted his shortcomings.

Iraola doesn't have the personnel to make the changes he has to make, so this win might just prove to be just that -- a good result -- rather than a sign of a tactical breakthrough.

Tighe: It's fine to walk away from this Liverpool performance still feeling deeply unconvinced by them. It's a measure of where they are right now, and how poor they were for the entirety of last season, that there are still many, many questions for Iraola and Co. to answer.

But let's face it: the bar is low for the Reds to impress right now; they really don't have to do much to get better week on week. That's what fans who spent all summer spinning out over a lack of transfer business are clinging onto right now, and exactly what the manager will point to at any opportunity.

I'll name a handful of those positives here: The attacking synergy between the front four looks like it's growing. Wirtz loves raw speed to play the ball into the path of and Barcola has it. Alexander Isak is impacting deep on the pitch. Jérémy Jacquet is looking more and more at home.

Unfortunately, there were two sides to Barcola's night: He made the right runs and his speed and directness brought Anfield to its feet, but he fluffed two major chances -- a noted, concerning weakness of his -- and came off injured late on.

Marcotti: I don't think this is going to be Iraola's team -- or, at least, the team Liverpool had in mind when they hired him and assembled this group of players -- for a while. It takes time for any manager and especially one whose movements and patterns of play are as distinct as Iraola's. Already we've seen him tone down some concepts to suit the players at his disposal.

On top of that, unlike his previous club Bournemouth, Iraola has to contend with European football too, which limits the time he has to work on the pitch. Furthermore, he's not playing with the guys he wans to work with, because Hugo Ekitike is still out. And I'm not even sure how much rational thinking has gone into this squad. He has three right back options -- Jeremie Frimpong, Ronald Araújo and Conor Bradley -- and they're all radically different from each other and radically different from the guy who played the position for Iraola at Bournemouth.

That said, it's three points against a very tough opponent and Liverpool showed character in coming from behind. Some guys -- Jacquet, Isak -- showed growth. I'm not sure you can carry the 4-2-3-1 with Szoboszlai as one of your two, but he's still probably Liverpool's most important player.

Q4. BARCELONA 5-1 FEYENOORD: Raphinha has picked up where he left off last season, scoring the kind of goal early on that kids dream of, putting two defenders on their backsides with one single move and then casually finishing. He has EIGHT goals already in just five Barça games, but ... are we sold on Barcelona? Their stats are gaudy -- five wins from five including their UCL opener, outscoring opponents by 22-3 -- but are we convinced by them?
Ogden: Barcelona are definitely a contender this season. Lamine Yamal is a year older and more experienced and Raphinha is flying again. The addition of Rodri could be the game-changer because he brings discipline and a defensive mindset to a very attack-minded team. Barca hammered Feyenoord and they will do that to all of the lower-ranked teams, especially on that huge pitch at Camp Lou.

But when it comes to the crunch, can they really defend well enough over two legs to beat PSG, Bayern or Arsenal? That's the big question about Hansi Flick's team and we won't know until the spring, but if they can, it will be because of Rodri just as much as Raphinha.

Dawson: Yes. Or at least as sold as you can be in early September. You can only judge a team on what they've done and Barcelona are averaging more than four goals a game. It won't last (at least the rest of Spain and Europe hope it won't) but it shows exactly what they're capable of. As Mark says, Rodri is a massive addition. He's the type of player who can control the tempo of a game -- knowing when to quicken it up and when to slow it down. His game management could be vital in the latter rounds. For now, though, he can just sit back and let Raphinha, Yamal and the rest run rings round defences.

Tighe: Raphinha is one of the stories of the matchday and, potentially, the story of the European season so far for me. He's been thrust up front for Barcelona largely because they fumbled the Julián Álvarez signing and waved goodbye to 36-year-old Robert Lewandowski this summer and ... well, wouldn't you know it? He's been unbelievable as the No. 9 so far.

It looks like he's been playing there all his life. He makes the right runs, times them well, deceives defenders and finishes sharply. His dummy to send those two Feyenoord defenders for a hotdog ... my word, what a sight that was in the pouring rain.

He won't carry Barca's attacking effort alone -- Yamal is still the starboy and Gabriel Jesus has made a goal-scoring start to his Camp Nou career -- and it will be interesting to see if he can keep up this pace (not necessarily goals per game, but just sheer level of impact on the pitch) as the striker. Opponents will steadily adjust to him, perhaps figure him out. What then?

It could make or break the first half of Barça's season, because no matter how much control they exert, there is going to be a couple of games where they need a terrible, awful, scuffed, scrappy finish to nick all three points. That's when a true striker steps forward.

Marcotti: The question is whether we're sold on Barcelona and for me the answer is easy: no. You can't be sold on anyone at this stage. And yes, it's true that you can only beat what's in front of you, but until you prove yourself against better opposition you haven't proved much. So, for me, I'll be sold when they show other aspects of their game against better opponents.

That said, sure, they look scary good. And I think it's hugely impressively how quickly a guy like Anthony Gordon, for example, has settled in. That's a credit to Flick. We knew Raphinha was going to be motivated after his World Cup injury (and Fermín López even more so after being left at home) but, again, how quickly they adapted to playing a striker-less system ... that's hugely impressive. As is the fact that guys like Pau Cubarsí and Yamal came out of the gates so strong. Wasn't the World Cup supposed to be thoroughly exhausting? Weren't we all told how it was going to take months for people to get back to form after playing in a World Cup? What happened to that?

Flick plays his way and, almost by definition, there will be tough times ahead. At some point, the front four will tire or miss a pressing rotation and then it's a ball over the top and there are only so many times Cubarsi and Gerard Martín can defend effectively in space. And when it happens, we'll be talking about the high line and all that stuff. (And, by the way, that's not something Rodri is going to fix all by himself.)

In terms of top-to-bottom talent, Barcelona are right up there. But it's still high-risk/high-reward football beyond how any other team in Europe play. Getting it to work regularly against very good teams is something they haven't shown yet.

stories.headline: 2026 FIBA Women's World Cup: Team USA and quarterfinal preview
stories.summary: The U.S. women and France remain front-runners as the knockout stage arrives in Berlin, but who else has impressed?
stories.body:
BERLIN -- The quarterfinals are set for the 2026 FIBA World Cup, with eight teams still in the hunt for a spot on the podium in Germany this weekend.

The United States, France and Belgium are the only countries still undefeated, though Italy tested the U.S. women in their second group game. The Americans eked out a 55-52 victory, their lowest-scoring World Cup performance since 1971.

Those three teams, along with Spain (2-1), punched their tickets to Thursday's quarterfinals. On Tuesday, Hungary beat Japan and Germany topped Korea to also secure spots in the final eight. On Wednesday, China secured its quarterfinal berth with a win over Puerto Rico, and the final spot went to Australia, which held off Italy in the final qualification showdown.

Here's what you need to know about how the United States has performed and how the rest of the field ranks as we turn the page to the knockout rounds.

Jump to:

AUS | BEL | CHN | FRA

GER | HUN | ESP | USA

Power Rankings | Team USA analysis

In what areas has Team USA been most impressive?
As is the case with other U.S. women's teams, the depth of talent continues to stand out. Coach Kara Lawson has started the five returning senior team players -- Napheesa Collier, Kahleah Copper, Chelsea Gray, Breanna Stewart and Jackie Young -- each game this tournament, meaning the likes of Caitlin Clark, Paige Bueckers, Aliyah Boston and Angel Reese are coming off the bench -- an enviable position to every other country in this event.

Watching the United States at its best -- as ESPN colleague Michael Voepel put it during the 94-61 win over China -- is like watching a movie in which every role is played by an Oscar winner. And if the U.S. women are getting stops, getting out in transition, sharing the ball and making the opponent pay on the other end, it's world-class basketball.

For the most part, each player on the roster has had some strong moments so far this tournament -- even after the vets struggled mightily most of the Italy game, they were the ones who made winning plays down the stretch to ensure the United States remained undefeated. The Young and Turnt crew don't always get everything perfect, but they have shown they belong. Having so many newcomers will pay dividends in the future in terms of experience, but Team USA will need them now to ensure the team goes home with a fifth consecutive World Cup gold medal.

Where have the Americans struggled?
The U.S. women aren't immune from defensive breakdowns, which isn't shocking given the team came together so last minute and chemistry is developing in real time. But the biggest concern is how the USA will generate offense when things don't come easily.

It's unlikely the U.S. women will score 55 points and shoot below 30% from the field again this tournament (or maybe even this decade) as they did against Italy. But the performance was eerily reminiscent of the France game from the 2024 Olympics, another close call but with a gold medal on the line.

The U.S. women's efficiency in this tournament has been much lower than we're used to seeing: 43.4%, ranking eighth, and a 29% accuracy from the 3-point arc (11th in the field) -- all while not generating a ton of looks from deep (23 per game).

This is where not having A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum -- two players very capable of going to get a bucket -- really hurts. Which players, or what combinations, will create offense if things become stagnant?

During TNT's FIBA World Cup studio show, three-time U.S. Olympic gold medalist Tina Charles said after the Italy game that she didn't see anyone pull Team USA together and essentially say, "Enough, get it together, let's end this now." With no Diana Taurasi or Wilson around, that's Stewart's or Gray's role moving forward, with their play on the court and in how they lead their teammates.

Next opponent: Quarterfinals vs. Hungary (5:30 a.m. ET Thursday)

How they've looked: The U.S. women are right where everyone expected them to be: undefeated and playing in the quarterfinals. But their path so far hasn't been without some struggles. Though two of the United States' group games -- victories over China and Czechia by 30-plus points each -- reflected the dominance we've come to expect, the 55-52 win against Italy neared catastrophe. It was Team USA's smallest margin of victory in the World Cup since 1979 and its first World Cup game decided by single digits since 2010.

The U.S. women rebounded by scoring more first-half points against Czechia (57) than they totaled against Italy, and they hope to bring that momentum into the knockout rounds. Eight players are averaging at least six points, and no one is averaging more than 12 (Young is the team leader with 11.3 PPG).

2. France (3-0)

How they've looked: France was considered the top challenger to U.S. entering the World Cup and still appears to be the biggest contender. In fact, the French have a strong argument to top this ranking, having outscored opponents by a tournament-best 127 points. Their defense gave the U.S. women fits at the Paris Olympics, but so far in Berlin, Les Bleues have scored at least 95 points each game, with dynamic duo Williams (the tournament's leading scorer with 18.7 PPG) and Johannes combining for 36 PPG.

How they've looked: Belgium predictably came out of Group C unscathed, winning each of its first three games by double figures. And just as expected, Meesseman has been one of the best players in the tournament, averaging 18.3 points, 8.0 rebounds, 5.3 assists and 1.7 blocks. Belgium is the better team on paper, but Germany will be playing with extra pride and a boisterous home crowd behind it in the quarterfinals.

4. Spain (2-1)

How they've looked: Spain looked poised to be one of the more exciting teams to take the court in Berlin but enters the quarterfinals with a 2-1 record after suffering a stunning loss to Mali in the second game of group play. The Spanish can still get to the podium for their fourth time in as many tournament appearances, but that kind of run would surely necessitate their young duo of Martin (17.3 PPG) and Fam (12.3 PPG) to play beyond their years in big moments.

How they've looked: It hasn't been the easiest ride for Sandy Brondello's team. Already missing Sami Whitcomb because of injury before the World Cup, Australia lost Smith 12 minutes into its first game in Berlin. She hasn't played since and on Thursday was ruled out for the remainder of the World Cup. After taking care of Puerto Rico and Turkiye, the Australians kept up with Belgium (a 80-68 loss) but had to beat a gritty Italy squad for a spot in the final eight.

6. China (3-1)

How they've looked: The World Cup has been a roller coaster for China. The team was routed by the U.S. in its first game, nearly lost to Czechia the next time out before pulling away in overtime and then put together a convincing 20-point win over Italy to close group play. China beat Puerto Rico on Wednesday in a qualifying game for the quarterfinals, and France -- a tough matchup -- awaits in the quarters. Han Xu has been their superstar, averaging 17.3 points, 11.3 rebounds and 2.7 assists.

7. Germany (3-1)

Next opponent: Quarterfinals vs. Belgium (11:45 a.m. ET Thursday)

How they've looked: After being trounced by Spain to open the tournament, Germany has won three straight, including Tuesday's clobbering of Korea to clinch a spot in the quarters. A quarterfinal appearance is a good step for a program appearing in only its second World Cup, but Germany is hoping it can capitalize on being a host and having a talented squad. Buhner has had a strong tournament, averaging a team-high 15.3 points.

8. Hungary (3-1)
Current WNBA players:

F Dorka Juhász, Minnesota Lynx

How they've looked: It has been a memorable World Cup for Hungary, which is appearing in the event for the first time since 1998. The team was throttled by France to start the tournament but hasn't lost since on its way to the quarterfinals. Though Juhász carried Hungary through group play with averages of 17 points and 12.3 rebounds, Reka Lelik was the team's star Tuesday, finishing with a game-high 23 points, eight rebounds and four assists against Japan.

Liverpool could make a bid to sign Crystal Palace's Adam Wharton as soon as January, while Manchester United target Lewis Hall has reportedly agreed a new contract with Newcastle United. Join us for the latest transfer news and rumors from around the globe.

Transfers home page | Men's summer grades | Women's grades

Trending rumors

- Liverpool are on high alert with midfielder Adam Wharton expected to leave Crystal Palace in one of the next two transfer windows, potentially as early as January, reports TEAMtalk. Liverpool have a long-standing admiration for the 22-year-old, even though they didn't make a move in this summer as they prioritised strengthening other areas of the pitch. stories.headline: EuroLeague sets Oct. 5 to vote on role in NBA Europe project
stories.summary: EuroLeague owners are set to meet on Oct. 5 in Milan, Italy to discuss whether to accept the NBA proposal and allow the league to be absorbed into NBA Europe or continue to operate as a separate league.
stories.body:
The EuroLeague owners are set to meet on Oct. 5 in Milan, Italy to discuss their future role in the NBA's October 2027 planned launch of a new European basketball league.

EuroLeague Basketball CEO Chus Bueno said the organization would compete alongside NBA Europe should they not form a partnership with the proposed FIBA-backed project.

"If we don't get a deal in Europe, we're going to compete in Europe ... that's the discussion that we had internally, and if we have to, we're ready," Bueno told Reuters last week.

"It has to be a partnership that works for both of us, not just for one of us.

"We know the NBA ⁠can help operate things, so we should follow the NBA and they should follow the local IP [brand value] of clubs because they've been on the ground for 100 years and they can bring also a lot to the table for the NBA."

The NBA has received finalized bids from more than 20 groups, sources familiar with the negotiations told ESPN in late June.

Viable groups submitted bids in all 12 target cities, sources said, with multiple bids topping $1 billion in select markets, including from more than 20 existing basketball and football clubs, many of which are EuroLeague teams.

The NBA Board of Governors meet next week.

According to Gazzetta dello Sport, the Oct. 5 owners' meeting is for EuroLeague clubs to discuss whether to accept the NBA proposal and allow the league to be absorbed into NBA Europe, or whether to decline and continue operating a league separate from NBA Europe.

"If you have two leagues ... this is going to create fragmentation of the value, institutionally but also commercially, in media rights, fan attendance," Bueno told Reuters.

"We both said that if we don't have a deal, we have to keep going with our plans. So, as you know, they keep going through the process, and I keep going with my plan."

NBA Europe would feature 16 teams competing in a round-robin regular season and a multi-round playoff format, which will culminate with a finals.

Christo Stavropoulos, manager of Olimpia Milano, the club that will host the Oct. 5 meeting said the NBA's absorption of EuroLeague is not a given.

"If another competition is added, fragmentation will follow. For me, as I've said a thousand times, the ideal would be to collaborate with the NBA," Stavropoulos told Gazzetta dello Sport. "But it can't be taken for granted that it will happen. If it doesn't happen now, those of us in the EuroLeague have very clear ideas about what we want for the future.

"You know: franchises, more teams in the competition ... basketball in Europe is growing a lot, the EuroLeague is growing. Many teams want to join; the coming years are going to be very important.

"We will make important decisions about the future at the board meeting. If it's without the NBA , so be it. We have our own path prepared."

During the Oct. 5 meeting, eight new league franchise are expected to be approved for operation, part of Bueno's EuroLeague expansion plan.

Should EuroLeague opt out of NBA Europe, Bueno's plan includes a large-scale transition to a closed franchise system and the expansion of the league to 24 teams, with 21 permanent franchises securing their spots for the 2027-2028 season.

stories.headline: Max Verstappen admits to McLaren, Mercedes talks before 'following heart' with Red Bull stay
stories.summary: Max Verstappen has admitted to serious talks with McLaren and Mercedes before agreeing his Red Bull extension last month.
stories.body:
Max Verstappen has admitted to serious talks with McLaren and Mercedes before agreeing his Red Bull extension last month.

Verstappen ended a long period of uncertainty about his future with the new Red Bull deal, announced ahead of his home race, the Dutch Grand Prix, which overwrote a deal lasting until 2028 with one running through to the end of 2030.

The existence of escape clauses in his old deal had allowed rumours of moves elsewhere to spread.

Verstappen has acknowledged that he explored options with rival teams before committing to a longer deal.

"Of course, any kind of chat you take seriously," Verstappen said in a BBC Sport interview when asked about how serious talks were with McLaren and Mercedes. "They're all very respectful chats. There's nothing wrong with that."

Verstappen has been with Red Bull for his entire Formula 1 career. The company signed him to a developmental deal in 2014 before handing him a debut with junior team Toro Rosso the following season.

He memorably won for Red Bull on his first appearance with the team after replacing Daniil Kvyat at the 2016 Spanish Grand Prix.

He spent five seasons at the team before winning his first championship in 2021, the first of four consecutive titles.

- Spanish Grand Prix: Everything you need to know about the Madring

- Red Bull sign Kimi Raikkonen's son Robin, 11

- Leclerc advice for Max vs. 100 drivers: Don't crash!

Verstappen pointed out he could have left Red Bull in those fallow years and ultimately opted to stay this time around as he believes Red Bull can be contenders again in future.

"I felt that staying was, for me, the right choice," he said. "You have to follow your heart. I could have run away very early on in my Red Bull career and gone somewhere else to try and win. If you have a little bit of patience, you do end up winning. I feel like that's my approach now as well."

Part of the uncertainty around Verstappen's future had been linked to his discontent with Formula 1's controversial new hybrid engines, which have shifted a lot of emphasis onto energy management and deployment.

Verstappen has labelled this "anti-racing" and likened the new F1 to Mario Kart.

F1 is making tweaks to the engines in 2027 and 2028 to lessen the importance of the electrical elements and Verstappen hopes this will lead to an improvement in how the racing feels.

"Hoping that it will be better in the future," he said. "Accepting where we are at the moment. Still the love for the sport. Not at the moment the driving. But the love for the sport.

"I love competition, naturally. I just hope that in the coming years, towards 2030, it can only get better. And to start to make the best of it, because these are the rules for the next four or five years."

stories.headline: Roosters great lifts lid on future, finals injury cloud
stories.summary: Daniel Tupou is close to resolving his contract status for 2027 as he aims to keep fit for the Sydney Roosters' premiership push.
stories.body:
Daniel Tupou's hopes of finishing his 15th year in the NRL with a premiership and lifting the Rugby League World Cup with Tonga hinge on his ability to manage a shoulder issue that has threatened to ruin his season.

As he revealed he was nearing a decision on whether he would play on with the Sydney Roosters next year, Tupou spoke of the gruelling rehabilitation process he has undergone to return to fitness for Sunday's qualifying final against Penrith.

The winger suffered a shoulder dislocation in a game against Newcastle in late July and opted against going under the knife in a bid to help the Roosters push towards their first premiership since 2019.

"If it does happen again then I have to go for surgery," Tupou told AAP.

"At the moment it's feeling great ... it was painful when it was just hanging out and my physio had to pop it back in.

"We had a baby this year so she (my wife) was a bit off with me that I wasn't able to help out, but she understands."

A recurrence of the injury in the NRL finals series would also deny Tupou the chance to sign off from his international career with a trophy.

The 35-year-old is Tonga's record tryscorer and has been a mainstay of the group that led the nation's giant strides when they reached the semi-finals of the 2017 World Cup.

"Surgery would probably put me out for the World Cup," he said.

"Nobody would have thought we'd do something like that (in 2017) and create something special for our little nation.

"It's awesome and something that I'll always be grateful to have been a part of.

"The opportunity to play at the World Cup will be an awesome experience but I'm not looking too far ahead."

Tupou is without a contract beyond this year but he and the Roosters have taken a relaxed approach to his future.

The winger, who is one of Trent Robinson's most-trusted performers, and the club's record tryscorer said: "I'm sorting that out with my manager.

"I've got to catch up with him in the next couple of days and sort it out by the end of the week.

"There's a couple of options there but it's about whatever fits best for myself and my family."

stories.headline: Top moments, highlights as Seahawks defeat Patriots in Super Bowl rematch
stories.summary: The 2026 NFL season opened with a rematch between last year's Super Bowl teams, the Seattle Seahawks and the New England Patriots. Here are all the highlights from the first game of the new season.
stories.body:
The Seattle Seahawks stormed back to defeat the New England Patriots 13-10 Wednesday night in the NFL's 2026 season opener.

The game seemed destined for overtime as the Patriots drove down the field and set up at the Seahawks' 16-yard line with 26 seconds left in the game. However, New England quarterback Drake Maye threw a costly interception, and Seattle held on to win -- no different than Super Bowl LX against the Patriots months earlier.

The Seahawks had an inauspicious start with starting quarterback Sam Darnold injured on the last play of its opening drive. Seattle then went scoreless in the first half, becoming the third defending Super Bowl champion to be shut out in the first half of their season opener and first since 1984, according to ESPN Research.

The momentum shifted late in the second half, however. New England went up 10-0, and Seattle responded with 13 straight points, including a 45-yard touchdown from wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba. The Seahawks picked off Maye on consecutive possessions in the fourth quarter, setting up scores.

Stepping in for Darnold, Seattle quarterback Drew Lock threw for 187 yards and one touchdown, while Smith-Njigba had eight receptions for 122 yards. Maye had 178 passing yards and one score, but three interceptions.

stories.body:
TORONTO -- Dániel Sallói had a tying goal in the 72nd minute and Emilio Aristizábal scored in second-half stoppage time to give Toronto FC a 2-1 victory over MLS frontrunner Nashville SC on Wednesday night.

Toronto (6-7-11) extended its unbeaten streak to seven games, going 3-0-4 in that span. It was Toronto's first win against Nashville since Sept. 18, 2021.

Nashville (16-3-5) had its unbeaten streak halted at six games.

Sallói headed in Theo Corbeanu's cross in front of the goal.

Aristizábal, who subbed in for striker Josh Sargent in the 75th, knocked in the winner from close range three minutes into extra time.

Nashville took a 1-0 lead in the fourth minute on an own goal by Niklas Dorsch, who was in the lineup for the first time since suffering a facial fracture on Aug. 19. It was Toronto's second straight game scoring an own goal.

Nashville faces Inter Miami CF and Lionel Messi in a top-of-table clash on Saturday, Toronto plays away against Orlando City SC.

stories.headline: Under pressure: those with the biggest questions to answer in the semis
stories.summary: Two cut-throat AFL semifinals. Two of four teams facing the end of the road. And that means a host of individuals, players and coaches are under pressure. Rohan Connolly looks at who has the biggest questions to answer.
stories.body:
Two cut-throat AFL semifinals. Two of four teams facing the end of the road. That's the equation. And that means a host of individuals, players, and coaches are ... under pressure (yep, that Queen/David Bowie classic's going through my head now, too).

Go on, put it on and click your fingers to that bassline while you read about those most under the pump on Friday and Saturday evening.

Justin Longmuir
You won't find too many better recent examples of one result so starkly changing the narrative surrounding an AFL coach than Fremantle's loss to Hawthorn last Thursday night. Longmuir and his team had done everything right this season until then. Yet the bottom line remains they now teeter on the edge of a straight sets exit at home with Longmuir copping plenty of critical flak. The Dockers' ball movement was stymied, they were inefficient, with 57 forward entries producing only five goals, and Hawthorn created space far too easily. The "lack of flexibility" accusation has also popped up again, along with more talk about costly poor starts. Fremantle lost a home final last year to Gold Coast. A third home finals defeat in a row could damage Longmuir's reputational stocks irreparably.

Jeremy Cameron
There may not be another player under as much pressure to perform on Friday night as the dual Coleman medallist, who has been goalless for a month, and five times in his last seven outings. Cameron took just one mark and had only nine disposals against Carlton last week, lacked any sort of physical presence, and was drifting up around the wing to pick up what few touches he could manage. Cameron managed two goals in Geelong's narrow Round 15 loss to Fremantle in Perth, but even then the Cats were held to the second-lowest score of their last 10 outings. Anything less this week, and there will be an awful lot of responsibility upon the likes of Shannon Neale and Patrick Dangerfield to find Cameron's missing goals.

Josh Treacy
What's that expression, one day a rooster the next a feather duster? On August 25, Fremantle's Josh Treacy was being feted as the All-Australian centre half-forward for 2026. Just over a week later, he was getting towelled up by the critics for being "destroyed" by Hawthorn key defender Josh Battle. Treacy had just four disposals, no marks and kicked just one late consolation goal. He hadn't had a kick until late in the last quarter and was accused of not attacking the contest with his usual physical presence. It doesn't get any easier this week for him, either, given that last time Fremantle met Geelong, Connor O'Sullivan held him to 2.2 from only nine disposals, picking up 16 himself, six intercept marks and a coaches' vote. Treacy needs to improve on that effort and last week's significantly.

Patrick Dangerfield
Hang on. How can the best player on the ground in last week's elimination final be under pressure the very next game he plays? Well, being the long-time acknowledged champion he is, the Brownlow medallist is always under the microscope to an extent. If "Danger" plays a blinder, Geelong will generally win. That's pressure of its own. But then there's the memory of last year. Prior to last Friday night, it was in the 2025 preliminary final against Hawthorn that Dangerfield delivered his best September performance with 31 disposals and three goals. And the following week? Unfortunately, his banged-up 35-year-old frame couldn't repeat the dose, delivering a strangely muted 10-disposal effort in the grand final loss to Brisbane. Now, 12 months older, can he back up one superlative September effort with another?

Murphy Reid
Last year's Rising Star and this year's All-Australian might be a bit of a soft target given what he's done in two seasons, that he's only recently turned 20 and last week played only his second AFL final, but Reid was one of the biggest disappointments in Fremantle's soft qualifying final performance. Whether missing the two games prior with a groin niggle has thrown him out of his stride is an interesting question, but his usually precise kicking was unusually off-target against the Hawks, and his off night was a major factor in Fremantle lacking so much of the spark the headbanded youngster has brought to the team and which had typified their season to date.

Lachie Neale
The dual Brownlow medallist was hardly the only Lion to have a poor one last week, but there's several reasons he's probably under more pressure than nearly all his teammates this week. Most obviously, given the widespread expectation that he's headed elsewhere in 2027, this could well be his final game for the club. Plus he and the other midfielders are coming off a pantsing by the Swans and, in Neale's case, Jai Serong. Even if the Lions are to get through this, Neale remains under pressure; Brisbane would face the all-conquering Hawks, before potentially the Swans again or an old September foe in Geelong, with tagger Oisin Mullin looming as another handbrake on the two-time Brownlow winner. Neale's record in finals overall is stellar, but Brisbane has seldom needed one of his best September performances more.

Matthew Nicks
OK, let's be clear, Nicks isn't going to lose his job if Adelaide can't pull an upset against Brisbane at the Gabba, even though he might have had the Crows not beaten the Bulldogs last week. But pressure? That hasn't suddenly evaporated just because a rested Adelaide beat a lesser-ranked opponent at home and gave Nicks his first finals win. The stigma of last year's straight sets elimination remains strong, the Crows won three fewer games this season and finished five spots lower on the ladder, and their record against the very best in 2026 is hardly inspiring, 2-5 against the top five, including a 52-point thumping at the hands of Saturday's opponent at the same venue. Victory this time would absolutely shore up Nicks' credentials. Another bad loss? The question marks will intensify.

Brisbane's key defenders
Saturday was a horror show for the whole Brisbane line-up, but no-one more than its defenders, and its talls in Harris Andrews, Darcy Gardiner and Ryan Lester specifically, with Sydney pair Charlie Curnow and Logan McDonald booting 11 goals between them. McDonald successfully curbed Andrews' intercepting ability and cashed in with half-a-dozen goals, and Curnow smashed Gardiner. And the equation doesn't get any easier this week with Adelaide's three-pronged tall forward set-up featuring Riley Thilthorpe, Taylor Walker and Darcy Fogarty, who StatMate tells us has kicked at least two goals in his last eight games. Ty Gallop surely is a good chance of returning at Gardiner's expense, or even second ruck Darcy Fort. But whatever selection strings coach Chris Fagan pulls, the Lions can't afford their key backs to be anywhere near that bad again.

You can read more of Rohan Connolly's work at FOOTYOLOGY.

stories.headline: Mac Allister stunner gives Liverpool win amid contract sadness
stories.summary: A day after revealing his disappointment over the lack of a new contract offer by Liverpool, Alexis Mac Allister delivered the perfect response with the winning goal in a 2-1 victory against Atlético Madrid in the Champions League on Wednesday.
stories.body:
A day after revealing his disappointment over the lack of a new contract offer by Liverpool, Alexis Mac Allister delivered the perfect response with the winning goal in a 2-1 victory against Atlético Madrid in the Champions League on Wednesday.

Mac Allister unleashed a ferocious strike from outside of the box as Liverpool came back from a goal down at Anfield.

The Argentina international, who joined Liverpool in 2023, raced away to celebrate in front of the home fans. It was in stark contrast to his somber tone ahead of the game when discussing the uncertainty over his position at the club.

"I try to be sincere. It helped me free myself up a bit," Mac Allister said to ESPN Argentina after Wednesday's win when asked about his pregame comments. "I'll always be the same person, right up to my last day here, whether it's two years, longer, or if I leave sooner. I'm going to give it my all until the very last day.

"I really enjoy being at this club, and I'm very happy living in the moment"

Mac Allister's contract runs until 2028, so there is no urgency for Liverpool to renew yet. But his goal five minutes after halftime was a reminder of his qualities, firing powerfully into the corner and beyond the reach of Atlético goalkeeper Jan Oblak.

"Normally when I'm in those positions I like to shoot," Mac Allister said. "It doesn't happen very often, but I'm happy because I love to score goals. Today, it was a nice goal and was important for the team as well, which is what I want."

Atlético had taken the lead through Marcos Llorente after 17 minutes, with the midfielder extending his remarkable goal-scoring run at Anfield.

It was his fifth goal in his past three visits to Merseyside, having famously scored twice as Atlético eliminated then-defending champions Liverpool from the tournament just before the COVID-19 lockdown in 2020.

Dominik Szoboszlai leveled in the 40th before Mac Allister's winner.

"I think we have an amazing team. We have quality, we have desire, and we have everything to be successful," Mac Allister said. "But we need to show it. We have to have everyone in the same page, and we can do great things."

The win was a first for Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola against Atlético manager Diego Simeone in any competition, having lost three times and drawn once against the Argentine coach.

Mac Allister's Argentina teammate Julián Álvarez started the game for Atlético after a turbulent offseason saw him try to force a move away from Atlético to join Barcelona.

Information from The Associated Press was used in this report.

stories.headline: Tottenham's Mykhailo Mudryk out until at least October with ankle injury - sources"
stories.summary: Mykhailo Mudryk is set to be sidelined until October at the earliest after suffering an ankle injury in training, sources have told ESPN.
stories.body:
Mykhailo Mudryk is set to be sidelined until October at the earliest after suffering an ankle injury in training, sources have told ESPN.

The 25-year-old suffered the setback earlier this week and is now wearing a protective boot on his left leg.

Mudryk secured a surprise a deadline day loan move from Chelsea to Tottenham and made his Spurs debut in Saturday's 0-0 draw at Nottingham Forest when introduced as a 74th-minute substitute.

That cameo was his first appearance since November 2024 following a dispute over a positive test for banned substance meldonium. Mudryk was initially handed a four-year suspension but the Ukraine international was cleared to play in July after his case was resolved with the Football Association.

Spurs boss Roberto De Zerbi worked with Mudryk at Shakhtar Donetsk and is hopeful of reviving the winger's career after a torrid time at Stamford Bridge.
